+Items are grouped by scope: User, Workspace (one group per folder in a multi-root workspace), and Built-in. @@ -91,6 +91,8 @@ Customization source-folder providers may assign an opaque workspace group ident

`AICustomizationSource` distinguishes local, user, extension, plugin, and built-in items. Source providers and workspace services apply their applicable discovery policy before view-model grouping. Filtering changes presentation only; it does not mutate the underlying customization.

+`AICustomizationScope` is the independent axis that answers who a customization applies to: `user`, `workspace`, or `application` (built into VS Code or the agent, shown as Built-in). Scope drives the primary grouping of every management section; storage source continues to drive what can be done with an item. Who supplied an item within its scope is a separate `origin`: a plugin, an extension, or an organization is shown as a nested row in that scope, and the agent's own items are tagged in Built-in. Extensions and organization customizations belong to the user unless a provider reports otherwise. Providers may set the scope, an origin, and a `syncedFromClient` delivery for items synced to a remote agent environment. When a provider omits the scope, the shared normalizer derives it from the source and identifies organization files from the default chat extension. Agent hosts state scope through the namespaced `vscode.customization.scope` metadata; clients treat its absence as unknown and never classify an unknown host item as built in. Overridden customizations are not listed: agent hosts omit them, and local discovery skips same-named duplicates and hides built-in skills that a user or workspace skill replaces. The legacy `remote-host` and `remote-client` group keys are delivery markers, not display groups.
Customization sources adapt their data into the shared item contract. The management model aggregates those items, applies harness and storage filters, and projects list items for the active section.
